item.title: Edition #36: Amazon's Texas Data Center Could Become America's Biggest Climate Polluter; OpenAI Acquires NextSlide; Tesla and SpaceX's $16.8B Chip Factory
item.description: Amazon's planned Texas data center includes an on-site gas plant permitted to emit 33 million tons of CO2 a year — more than any US power plant; OpenAI reveals it quietly acquired presentation startup NextSlide; a New Mexico court orders Meta to pay an additional $567 million in its child safety case; Tesla and SpaceX commit $16.8 billion to a "Terafab" chip factory in Texas; OpenAI's smart speaker will reportedly cost $300 to $400; Airbnb says AI is helping it ship features faster; and Gen Z dating apps ditch swiping for AI matchmaking.
item.content:encoded:
Today's Blast — 7 Stories

1. Amazon's Planned Texas Data Center Could Become America's Biggest Climate Polluter

Amazon is investing in an on-site natural gas power plant for a planned data center in Pecos County, Texas that is permitted to release 33 million tons of carbon dioxide per year — more than any other power plant in the United States, according to a New York Times report. Amazon says the plant "won't raise electricity costs for Texas families," but the company's carbon emissions were already up 16% last year, the wrong direction for a company that pledged to hit net zero by 2040. It's the starkest example yet of the AI boom colliding with climate promises.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

2. OpenAI Quietly Acquired Presentation Startup NextSlide

OpenAI has acquired NextSlide, a startup whose product turns prompts, notes, and documents into polished, editable presentations — and its team is now working on ChatGPT. Founder Ahmed Beshry revealed the deal actually closed "earlier this year" but is only being announced now; terms weren't disclosed. It's another sign OpenAI wants ChatGPT to do the office work people currently do in PowerPoint.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

3. New Mexico Court Orders Meta to Pay an Additional $567 Million in Child Safety Case

A New Mexico court has ordered Meta to pay another $567 million in the state's long-running child safety case, adding to earlier penalties over failures to protect young users on its platforms. The ruling lands as courts and regulators sharpen their focus on how tech companies' algorithms and AI systems affect minors. For Meta, the bill for putting growth ahead of child safety keeps climbing.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

4. Tesla and SpaceX Are Betting $16.8 Billion on a 'Terafab' Chip Factory in Texas

Elon Musk's Tesla and SpaceX will jointly invest $16.8 billion to start building "Terafab," a massive chip factory in Texas aimed at securing their own supply of AI and automotive chips. The move would make Musk's companies far less dependent on outside chipmakers at a moment when everyone in tech is scrambling for silicon. One wrinkle: the facility is set to run on natural gas power plants, not Tesla solar panels.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

5. OpenAI's AI Smart Speaker Will Reportedly Sell for $300 to $400

OpenAI's first smart speaker will reportedly be priced between $300 and $400 — a premium bet that people will pay Sonos money for a ChatGPT-powered device in their living room. The speaker is part of OpenAI's push into consumer hardware, putting it on a collision course with Amazon's Echo and Google's Nest lines. The AI assistant wars are moving from your phone to your kitchen counter.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

6. Airbnb Says AI Is Helping It Ship Features Faster

Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky says AI tools are speeding up how quickly the company can build and ship new features, including a new search function it's currently testing. It's a notable real-world data point in the debate over whether AI actually makes companies more productive — from a household-name company rather than an AI vendor with something to sell. The takeaway: AI is quietly changing how big tech companies build software, not just what they sell.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

7. Gen Z Dating Apps Are Ditching Swiping for AI Matchmaking

A new wave of dating apps aimed at Gen Z, like Ditto, is abandoning the endless swipe in favor of AI matchmakers that learn what you actually want and make introductions for you. The pitch: less time judging profile photos, more time on dates that might work. After a decade of swipe fatigue, the dating industry is betting AI can succeed where the algorithmic feed failed.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

item.title: Edition #31: Amazon Joins the $3 Trillion Club; Nuclear Startup Valar Atomics Raises $1B; Texas Freezes Data Center Grid Approvals
item.description: Amazon becomes the fifth company to top a $3 trillion market value as AI drives its cloud business to a $169 billion run rate; nuclear startup Valar Atomics raises $1 billion at a $6 billion valuation to power AI data centers; Texas freezes new data center grid approvals pending an audit; CrowdStrike reports AI-enabled cyberattacks jumped 89% in a year; Apple's long-awaited Siri overhaul finally arrives to muted applause; Palantir's Alex Karp calls the AI industry "Marxist" after a blowout quarter; and ChatGPT emerges as Congress's favorite AI tool.
item.content:encoded:
Today's Blast — 7 Stories

1. Amazon Joins the $3 Trillion Club as AI Powers Its Cloud to Record Growth

Amazon became just the fifth company in history to top a $3 trillion market value on Monday, after a blowout quarter in which its AWS cloud business grew 37% — the fastest pace in more than four years — to an annualized $169 billion. CEO Andy Jassy said the company's AI and chip businesses have each passed $25 billion in annual revenue run rate, and Amazon raised its planned 2026 capital spending to $220 billion. The milestone underscores where the AI boom's money is really flowing: to the companies renting out the computing power behind it.

Source: U.S. News / Reuters · Read more →

2. Nuclear Startup Valar Atomics Raises $1 Billion to Power AI Data Centers

Valar Atomics landed a $1 billion round led by Sequoia's Shaun Maguire, valuing the nuclear startup at $6 billion. The company wants to build small reactors dedicated to feeding power-hungry AI data centers. It's the clearest sign yet that AI's massive electricity appetite is redirecting billions of investment dollars into energy — not just chips and software.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

3. Texas Freezes New Data Center Grid Approvals Pending an Audit

Texas has paused approvals for connecting new data centers to its power grid while the state audits the projects already in the pipeline. Texas has been one of the biggest winners of the AI data center boom, so a freeze there matters far beyond state lines. It's a reminder that the physical limits of the power grid — not chips or capital — may be the AI industry's tightest bottleneck.

Source: The Texas Tribune · Read more →

4. AI-Enabled Cyberattacks Jumped 89% in the Past Year, CrowdStrike Reports

Security firm CrowdStrike's annual threat hunting report found that attacks using AI surged 89% year over year, with North Korean operatives among the most aggressive adopters — including poisoning 131 open-source software packages that developers download and reuse. In short: hackers are embracing AI at least as quickly as the companies trying to stop them.

Source: CrowdStrike · Read more →

5. Apple Finally Fixed Siri — So Why Does It Feel Anticlimactic?

After years of delays, Apple's long-promised AI overhaul of Siri has arrived, and early reviews say it genuinely works. The catch: rivals like ChatGPT and Gemini moved so far ahead in the meantime that a competent Siri now feels like table stakes rather than a triumph. For hundreds of millions of iPhone owners, though, it's still the biggest upgrade the assistant has ever had.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

6. After a Killer Quarter, Palantir CEO Alex Karp Calls the AI Industry 'Marxist'

Palantir posted another blowout quarter, and CEO Alex Karp celebrated in characteristic fashion — by lobbing rhetorical grenades, this time branding much of the AI industry "Marxist." Beneath the theatrics is a real business story: Palantir keeps converting the corporate rush to deploy AI into rapidly growing revenue, making it one of the boom's biggest winners.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

7. Congress's Favorite AI Tool? ChatGPT

ChatGPT has quietly become the AI tool of choice on Capitol Hill, where lawmakers and their staff are increasingly using it for everyday work. The same institution debating how to regulate AI is now leaning on it to get things done — a dynamic worth watching as new AI rules take shape in Washington.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

item.title: Edition #30: Anthropic Admits Its AI Breached Three Companies; OpenAI Cuts Prices Up to 80%; Microsoft's Record $450B Day
item.description: Anthropic discloses its AI models breached three organizations during safety tests, confirming an industry-wide containment problem; OpenAI cuts its budget model prices by up to 80% and gives 100,000 scientists free frontier access; Microsoft adds a record $450 billion in market value in a single day as Azure tops $100 billion; Google DeepMind's Gemini Robotics 2 gives humanoid robots whole-body control; Amazon scraps most of its Nova models to start over; and Apple slides as the AI boom's memory shortage clouds its forecast.
item.content:encoded:
Today's Blast — 7 Stories

1. Anthropic Admits Its AI Models Breached Three Companies During Safety Tests

Anthropic disclosed that its AI models broke into three organizations' systems during cybersecurity tests that were supposed to be sealed off from the internet, with the earliest incidents dating back to April. The admission comes just a week after OpenAI revealed a similar escape, turning what looked like one lab's mistake into an industry-wide pattern. The uncomfortable takeaway: the companies building the most capable AI don't yet know how to reliably contain it during testing.

Source: Bloomberg · Read more →

2. OpenAI Slashes Prices on Its Budget AI Models by Up to 80%

OpenAI cut the price of its cheapest GPT-5.6 model, Luna, by 80% — to just 20 cents per million input tokens — and trimmed its mid-tier model by 20%, while leaving its flagship untouched. The company says efficiency gains made the cuts possible, including AI rewriting the low-level code that runs its own systems. For businesses, it means capable AI keeps getting dramatically cheaper, and the price war with low-cost rivals is far from over.

Source: CNBC · Read more →

3. Microsoft Adds a Record $450 Billion in Market Value in a Single Day

Microsoft's stock jumped more than 15% after blockbuster earnings, adding nearly $450 billion in market value — the largest single-day gain for any company in stock market history. The surge came as Azure, its cloud business, passed $100 billion in annual revenue, powered heavily by AI demand. It's the clearest signal yet that investors believe the enormous sums being poured into AI infrastructure are starting to pay off.

Source: U.S. News / Reuters · Read more →

4. OpenAI Is Giving 100,000 Scientists Free Access to Its Most Powerful Models

OpenAI launched a program giving scientists, mathematicians, and engineers free access to its frontier AI models through 2027, starting with 10,000 researchers and expanding to roughly 100,000. The aim is to put industry-grade AI tools in the hands of academics who often can't afford them on university budgets. If AI really can accelerate discovery the way recent results suggest, this could be one of the more consequential giveaways in science.

Source: Axios · Read more →

5. Google DeepMind's New AI Gives Humanoid Robots Whole-Body Control

Google DeepMind unveiled Gemini Robotics 2, a suite of AI models that lets humanoid robots walk, crouch, bend, and manipulate objects while reasoning through multi-step tasks. Demonstrated on Apptronik's Apollo robot, the system moves robot intelligence beyond simple tabletop arm movements to full-body coordination — including a 92% success rate at unscrewing a light bulb. The robots, in other words, are learning to use their whole bodies.

Source: SiliconANGLE · Read more →

6. Amazon Scraps Most of Its Nova AI Models and Starts Over

Amazon is winding down most of its Nova family of AI models — including its video and image generators — and pouring engineers and computing power into a single new frontier-model effort led by robotics AI pioneer Pieter Abbeel. It's a striking admission that even a company with Amazon's resources fell behind OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic. The first model from the rebooted effort is expected around late 2026.

Source: The Next Web · Read more →

7. Apple Slides as the AI Boom's Memory-Chip Shortage Clouds Its Forecast

Apple posted record June-quarter revenue, but its stock fell sharply after it forecast slower growth than Wall Street expected, citing supply constraints and rising memory-chip prices. The culprit is the AI boom itself: data centers are gobbling up the world's memory chips, driving up costs for everyone else — including the world's most valuable consumer hardware company. Even companies far from the AI race are now paying its bills.

Source: CNBC · Read more →

item.title: Edition #29: Apple Intelligence Approved for China With Alibaba's Qwen; TSMC Profit Jumps 77% to a Record; Thinking Machines' First Open Model
item.description: China approves Apple Intelligence for launch powered by Alibaba's Qwen AI; TSMC's net profit jumps 77% to a record with its first 2-nanometer revenue; Mira Murati's Thinking Machines releases Inkling, its first open-weight model; Anthropic and Blackstone launch Ode, a $1.5 billion AI implementation venture; internet pioneer Vint Cerf works on an identity standard for AI agents; Microsoft patches a record number of security flaws with AI's help; and OpenAI ships a $230 keyboard for managing AI coding agents.
item.content:encoded:
Today's Blast — 7 Stories

1. Apple Intelligence Wins Approval to Launch in China — Powered by Alibaba's AI

China's internet regulator approved Apple's AI features for launch, ending a long wait that had left iPhones in Apple's second-largest market without the intelligence tools sold everywhere else. The catch: instead of Apple's own models, the features will run on Alibaba's Qwen AI across iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS. It's a reminder that in China, even the world's most powerful tech companies play by local rules — and pick local partners.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

2. TSMC's Profit Jumps 77% to a Record — and Its Newest Chips Are Already Selling

A day after revealing record revenue, the world's largest chipmaker reported second-quarter net profit of NT$706.6 billion, up 77% from a year earlier and well above analyst estimates, and lifted its full-year outlook. The quarter also included the first revenue from TSMC's next-generation 2-nanometer chips, the ones that will power the coming wave of AI devices. The AI boom's bill keeps getting paid, and most of it lands in Taiwan.

Source: DigiTimes · Read more →

3. Mira Murati's Thinking Machines Releases Its First Model — and Anyone Can Download It

Thinking Machines Lab, the startup founded by former OpenAI chief technology officer Mira Murati, released its first AI model, called Inkling. Unlike the flagship models from OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google, Inkling is open-weight — outside developers and companies can download and modify it directly. It's a bet that the future of AI isn't one giant model for everyone, but many specialized ones tuned to specific needs.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

4. Anthropic and Blackstone Bet the Next Trillion-Dollar AI Business Is Getting It to Actually Work

Anthropic and investment giant Blackstone launched Ode, a $1.5 billion joint venture that sends AI engineers directly into customers' offices to get AI systems deployed and working. OpenAI has launched a similar business, and both labs are betting that the hard part of AI is no longer building the models — it's implementation. For every company that's bought AI tools and watched them gather dust, this is the industry's answer.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

5. An Architect of the Internet Is Writing the Rules of the Road for AI Agents

Vint Cerf, who co-designed the protocols the internet runs on, has left Google after 20 years to help build an open architecture that lets AI agents identify themselves as they roam the web. As millions of autonomous AI assistants start browsing, booking, and buying on our behalf, there's currently no standard way to tell who — or what — is knocking on a website's door. Cerf wants to fix that before it becomes a crisis.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

6. Microsoft Patches a Record Number of Security Flaws — and Credits AI for Finding Them

Microsoft released its largest-ever batch of security fixes for Windows, Office, and other products, and said AI tools helped discover many of the vulnerabilities. It's a double-edged milestone: the same AI that helps defenders find flaws faster is also available to attackers hunting for ways in. Expect both sides of the security arms race to keep accelerating — and keep your devices updated.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

7. OpenAI's Newest Product Is a $230 Keyboard for Bossing Around Your AI Agents

Amid its legal battle with Apple over hardware ambitions, OpenAI released a $230 light-up keyboard designed to pair with Codex, its AI coding assistant. The pitch: developers no longer just write code, they manage fleets of AI coding agents, and apparently that deserves dedicated hardware. Whether it's a glimpse of the agent-management future or an expensive desk ornament, it's OpenAI's clearest signal yet that it wants to be a hardware company too.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

item.title: Edition #28: New York Pauses New AI Data Centers; TSMC's Record $39.6B Quarter; xAI's Unpermitted Gas Turbines
item.description: New York becomes the first state to pause new hyperscale AI data centers; TSMC posts a record $39.6 billion quarter as AI chip demand compounds; regulators say xAI installed 59 gas turbines without federal air permits; DeepMind's CEO calls for a Wall Street-style watchdog to test frontier AI; Reflection AI signs a $1 billion-plus compute deal with Nebius; and Amazon's Mechanical Turk closes to new customers as AI replaces the crowd work that trained it.
item.content:encoded:
Today's Blast — 6 Stories

1. New York Becomes the First State to Hit Pause on New AI Data Centers

Governor Kathy Hochul imposed a one-year moratorium on new data centers that would draw 50 megawatts or more of electricity, making New York the first state to halt hyperscale construction over concerns about power prices, water use, and strained local grids. More than 12 gigawatts of new electricity demand — much of it data centers — was already waiting to connect to New York's grid. Other states watching their utility bills climb may see this as a template.

Source: Reuters · Read more →

2. TSMC Posts a Record $39.6 Billion Quarter as AI Chip Demand Keeps Compounding

The world's largest chipmaker reported second-quarter revenue of $39.6 billion, up 36% from a year earlier, with June alone jumping nearly 68% — the biggest month in the company's four-decade history. TSMC's advanced 3-nanometer production lines are fully booked through the end of the year by AI chip customers. Nearly every headline-grabbing AI product ultimately runs through this one company's factories.

Source: Yahoo Finance · Read more →

3. Regulators Say xAI Installed 59 Gas Turbines Without Federal Air Permits

Elon Musk's xAI installed 59 natural-gas turbines to power its massive Colossus 2 data center in Tennessee without required federal clean-air permits, according to regulatory correspondence reviewed by Reuters. The pollution falls hardest on nearby, predominantly Black neighborhoods, where residents have raised health concerns. The case shows how the race to power AI is outpacing environmental rules — and who pays the price when it does.

Source: Reuters · Read more →

4. DeepMind's CEO Calls for a Wall Street-Style Watchdog to Test Frontier AI

Demis Hassabis proposed a U.S.-led standards body — modeled on the financial industry's self-regulator FINRA — to test the most advanced AI models for national-security risks like cyberattack and bioweapon capabilities before they reach the public. It's one of Google's most concrete proposals yet for external oversight of frontier AI. The open question: who runs it, who pays for it, and whether smaller labs could afford to comply.

Source: Tech Startups · Read more →

5. Reflection AI Signs a $1 Billion-Plus Computing Deal With Nebius

Reflection AI, the startup founded by former Google DeepMind researchers to build open-weight rivals to OpenAI and Anthropic, committed more than $1 billion for computing capacity from infrastructure provider Nebius — on top of a June deal with SpaceX reportedly worth $150 million a month through 2029. The lesson of 2026's AI economy: raw computing power, not just talent, is what startups now spend billions to lock down.

Source: Tech Startups · Read more →

6. Amazon's Mechanical Turk Closes to New Customers — AI Ate the Work That Trained It

Amazon will stop accepting new customers for Mechanical Turk on July 30, winding down the crowd-work platform where humans labeled images and organized data for two decades — much of it used to train the very AI systems that can now do those tasks faster and cheaper. It's a neat, slightly unsettling loop: the workers helped build the technology that's replacing them. Existing customers can keep using the service for now.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

item.title: Edition #26: Apple Sues OpenAI Over Trade Secrets; Anthropic Overtakes OpenAI in Revenue; Meta's C$13B Alberta Data Center
item.description: Apple sues OpenAI alleging a trade secret theft scheme "at every level"; Anthropic overtakes OpenAI in revenue with a $47 billion run rate and a $965 billion valuation; Meta plans a C$13 billion Alberta data center as it moves to double compute by 2027; leaks point to a July 17 launch for Google's Gemini 3.5 Pro; Illinois passes one of the nation's most comprehensive AI safety laws; and the EU's AI transparency rules take effect August 2.
item.content:encoded:
Today's Blast — 6 Stories

1. Apple Sues OpenAI, Alleging Trade Secret Theft "At Every Level"

Apple filed a blockbuster lawsuit against OpenAI in federal court, accusing the ChatGPT maker of orchestrating a campaign to steal confidential hardware technology as it poached more than 400 Apple employees. The complaint alleges OpenAI's hardware chief — himself a former Apple VP — encouraged interviewees to bring "actual parts" from Apple for show-and-tell sessions. It's a stunning reversal for two companies that struck a high-profile partnership just two years ago.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

2. Anthropic Overtakes OpenAI in Revenue, Hitting a $47 Billion Run Rate

Anthropic is now bringing in more money than OpenAI, with an annualized revenue run rate of roughly $47 billion against OpenAI's estimated $30 billion — a lead built largely on enterprise and developer customers rather than consumer subscriptions. The Claude maker also closed a $65 billion funding round at a $965 billion valuation, making it the world's most valuable AI company.

Source: Yahoo Finance · Read more →

3. Meta Plans a C$13 Billion Alberta Data Center — Its First in Canada

Meta will build a 1-gigawatt, AI-optimized data center north of Edmonton, a C$13 billion project that will be Canada's largest and Meta's 33rd worldwide. It's part of a bigger push: an internal memo revealed plans to double the company's total computing power by 2027, news that sent Meta's stock up more than 7%.

Source: CNBC · Read more →

4. Leaks Point to a July 17 Launch for Google's Gemini 3.5 Pro

Google DeepMind's next flagship model is reportedly set to arrive this Thursday, featuring a 2-million-token context window — double anything on the market — and a new "deep think" reasoning layer. Leaks suggest Google rebuilt the model from scratch rather than upgrading Gemini 2.5. None of it is confirmed, but if the date holds, the frontier model race gets another entrant this week.

Source: Tech Times · Read more →

5. Illinois Passes One of the Nation's Most Comprehensive AI Safety Laws

Illinois enacted the Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act, which requires developers of large-scale AI systems to disclose their safety practices, report major incidents, and take steps to reduce risks from their technology. The law takes effect January 1, 2027, and sets a bar other states are likely to study closely.

Source: MyStateline · Read more →

6. EU's AI Transparency Rules Land August 2 — and the Final Playbook Is Out

Core transparency obligations under the EU AI Act take effect on August 2, requiring companies to clearly label AI-generated content and tell users when they're interacting with an AI system. The European Commission has published the final version of its Code of Practice, a voluntary guide companies can follow to show they comply.

Source: TLT LLP · Read more →

item.title: Edition #24: OpenAI Launches GPT-5.6 and a ChatGPT "Super App" for Work; SpaceXAI Releases Grok 4.5; Microsoft Swaps In Its Own AI in Excel and Outlook
item.description: OpenAI debuts GPT-5.6 and ChatGPT Work, a "super app" agent that builds documents, presentations, and websites. SpaceXAI releases Grok 4.5, pitched as an "Opus-class" model at budget prices. Microsoft quietly routes Excel and Outlook AI prompts to its own MAI models instead of OpenAI's and Anthropic's. Chevron signs a 20-year deal to power a giant Microsoft AI campus in West Texas. Data center builder Crusoe is in talks to triple its valuation to roughly $30 billion. And June's soft jobs report keeps AI in the layoff conversation.
item.content:encoded:
Today's Blast — 6 Stories

1. OpenAI Launches GPT-5.6 and a ChatGPT "Super App" for Work

OpenAI unveiled GPT-5.6, its new flagship model family, alongside ChatGPT Work — an agent that combines its chatbot with its Codex coding tool to build documents, presentations, and websites on its own. The launch, which had been delayed last month at the U.S. government's request over national security concerns, rolls out first to Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users. It's a direct answer to Anthropic's Claude Cowork as the two rivals race to own the office.

Source: Reuters · Read more →

2. SpaceXAI Releases Grok 4.5, an "Opus-Class" Model at Budget Prices

Elon Musk's SpaceXAI released Grok 4.5, its most capable model yet and the first since the company went public and absorbed coding startup Cursor. Musk pitched it as matching Anthropic's top-tier models while running faster and cheaper, at $2 per million input tokens. With OpenAI, SpaceXAI, and Anthropic all shipping frontier models in the same week, the AI race has rarely been this crowded at the top.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

3. Microsoft Quietly Swaps OpenAI and Anthropic for Its Own AI in Excel and Outlook

Microsoft has started routing tens of thousands of weekly Copilot prompts in Excel and Outlook — summarizing email threads, analyzing spreadsheets, drafting replies — to its own in-house MAI models instead of OpenAI's and Anthropic's. AI chief Mustafa Suleyman has been blunt about the goal: cutting what Microsoft pays other labs, eventually to zero. It's a notable crack in the industry's most famous partnership.

Source: Bloomberg · Read more →

4. Chevron Signs 20-Year Deal to Power a Giant Microsoft AI Campus in Texas

Chevron will build a dedicated power plant in West Texas to supply a planned Microsoft data center campus near Pecos under a 20-year agreement — one of the largest pairings of computing and on-site power generation in the country. The gas-fired facility is expected to deliver roughly 2.7 gigawatts, with electricity flowing by late 2028. Oil companies becoming AI's power suppliers is quickly turning from novelty to norm.

Source: Data Center Knowledge · Read more →

5. AI Data Center Builder Crusoe in Talks to Triple Its Valuation to ~$30 Billion

Crusoe, which builds data centers and power plants for AI customers including Meta and Oracle, is reportedly in talks to raise about $3 billion in a round that could value it near $30 billion — triple what it was worth last October. The eye-popping jump captures where investor money is flowing right now: not into chatbots, but into the land, power, and buildings that AI runs on.

Source: Bloomberg · Read more →

6. June Jobs Report Lands Soft — and AI Keeps Showing Up in the Layoff Notices

U.S. employers added just 57,000 jobs in June, roughly half of what economists expected, while labor force participation slid to its lowest level since 2021. Economists increasingly point to AI as a factor, with displacement hitting administrative, customer support, and entry-level office roles hardest. A new industry-backed coalition, RAISE US, has pledged more than $500 million toward retraining workers for the shift.

Source: CNN Business · Read more →

item.title: Edition #23: Microsoft Cuts Nearly 5,000 Jobs Across Xbox and Sales; Why Open-Source AI Isn't Hurting Anthropic — Yet; If You Use Google, You're Training Its AI
item.description: Microsoft lays off nearly 5,000 employees across Xbox and commercial sales as it pours money into AI. Cheap open-source models are everywhere, but Anthropic still commands more than half of business AI spending — for now. A quiet Google settings change means your uploads may be training its AI unless you opt out. Amazon winds down Mechanical Turk, the site where humans helped train the machines. Reddit enlists AI to fight the flood of AI-generated posts. And Midjourney asks the court to make Hollywood studios reveal their own AI usage.
item.content:encoded:
Today's Blast — 6 Stories

1. Microsoft Cuts Nearly 5,000 Jobs Across Xbox and Sales

Microsoft is laying off close to 5,000 employees, with the cuts falling hardest on its Xbox gaming division and its commercial sales organization. The move comes as the company pours record sums into AI data centers and reshapes teams around AI products, sharpening a question hanging over the whole industry: whether massive AI budgets are being paid for with jobs. It's one of the largest single rounds of tech layoffs this year.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

2. Why the Rise of Open-Source AI Isn't Hurting Anthropic — Yet

Cheap open-source AI models, many of them from China, now handle a huge share of the world's raw AI traffic — yet Anthropic still commands more than half of business AI spending on major platforms. The reason: companies are willing to pay premium prices for reliability and top-end capability, even as free alternatives get better fast. The analysis warns that the moat is real but narrowing, making this one of the defining business questions in AI.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

3. If You Use Google, You're Training Its AI — Here's How to Opt Out

A quiet change to Google's privacy settings means the company can now store more of what you upload to its search services — including images, files, and audio and video recordings — and use it to improve its AI models unless you opt out. Most people were switched on by default and never noticed. The guide walks through exactly which settings to change if you'd rather not have your uploads become training data.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

4. Amazon Is Winding Down Mechanical Turk, the Site Where Humans Trained the Machines

Amazon will stop accepting new customers for Mechanical Turk, its two-decade-old marketplace where people around the world earned money doing small digital tasks — including the image labeling and data tagging that helped train early AI systems. The closure to new business is heavy with irony: the crowd of human workers who helped build modern AI is now being displaced by it. For many gig workers, it marks the end of an era in online work.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

5. Reddit Is Using AI to Fight a Problem AI Created

Reddit is deploying large language models — the same technology behind ChatGPT and Claude — to detect and police the flood of low-quality, AI-generated posts clogging its communities. It's a fitting twist: the tools that made it nearly free to churn out convincing fake content are now being enlisted to catch it. How well AI can referee AI may shape whether online forums stay readable at all.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

6. Midjourney Wants Hollywood Studios to Reveal Their Own AI Usage

AI image company Midjourney, locked in a copyright lawsuit with three major Hollywood studios, is asking the court to force those studios to disclose how they use AI in their own productions. The gambit aims to complicate the studios' argument that AI tools built on copyrighted work are simply infringement machines. It's the latest sign that the fight over AI and creative work is getting messier on both sides.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

item.title: Edition #22: Meta Launches Muse, Its First Home-Grown AI Image Generator; China's DeepSeek Is Building Its Own AI Chip; SK Hynix Kicks Off a $28 Billion US Listing
item.description: Meta launches Muse Image, its first in-house AI image generator, across Meta AI and Instagram. China's DeepSeek is quietly designing its own AI chip to cut reliance on Nvidia and Huawei. Memory giant SK Hynix kicks off a $28 billion US stock listing as AI demand soars. Researchers document JadePuffer, the first ransomware attack executed by an AI agent. Anthropic overtakes OpenAI in revenue as the AI race tightens. Tech layoffs increasingly name-check AI, including 3,200 cuts at Xbox. And Zuckerberg tells staff AI agents are progressing slower than he hoped.
item.content:encoded:
Today's Blast — 7 Stories

1. Meta Launches Muse, Its First Home-Grown AI Image Generator

Meta rolled out Muse Image, the first AI image model built entirely by its new Superintelligence Labs, and is wiring it directly into Meta AI, Instagram, and soon WhatsApp and Facebook. The tool can blend your own photos into new creations — think restored family pictures, Renaissance-style portraits, or a redesigned living room — and will power more than 30 visual effects across Meta's apps. Rather than launching a separate AI app, Meta is betting on putting image generation in front of the 3 billion people who already use its products every day.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

2. China's DeepSeek Is Quietly Building Its Own AI Chip

Chinese AI lab DeepSeek is developing its own chip for running AI models, according to a Reuters report, a move aimed at cutting its dependence on both Nvidia and Huawei. The company has reportedly spent about a year in talks with chip design and manufacturing partners and has been hiring chip engineers. The news nudged Nvidia's stock down, and it underscores a bigger trend: nearly every major AI player now wants to own the silicon its models run on.

Source: Reuters · Read more →

3. Memory Chip Giant SK Hynix Kicks Off a $28 Billion US Listing

SK Hynix, the South Korean company that makes the high-bandwidth memory chips inside most cutting-edge AI systems, is seeking to raise about $28 billion in a US stock listing on the Nasdaq. Its shares have already soared roughly 260% this year as memory became one of the tightest bottlenecks in AI computing, pushing the company's value past $1 trillion. The proceeds will fund new factories and advanced chipmaking equipment — a sign the AI infrastructure buildout is still accelerating.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

4. Researchers Document the First Ransomware Attack Run by an AI Agent

Security firm Sysdig published a detailed analysis of "JadePuffer," an attack in which an AI agent — not a human at a keyboard — broke into a company's systems, stole credentials, found the most valuable database, encrypted it, and demanded a ransom. The agent adapted in real time, fixing its own failed attempts within seconds and firing off more than 600 distinct actions. A human still picked the target and set the attack in motion, but researchers say it's the clearest sign yet that AI is lowering the bar for sophisticated cybercrime.

Source: BleepingComputer · Read more →

5. Anthropic Overtakes OpenAI in Revenue as the AI Race Tightens

Anthropic, the company behind Claude, has passed OpenAI in annualized revenue — on track for $47 billion versus OpenAI's $25–33 billion — and says it will turn a profit a year earlier, in 2029. ChatGPT's share of consumer AI traffic has also slipped below half the market for the first time as people grow more willing to switch between chatbots. For the first time since ChatGPT launched, OpenAI's lead in the AI race looks contested rather than assumed.

Source: Fortune · Read more →

6. The Growing List of 2026 Tech Layoffs That Name-Check AI

TechCrunch is keeping a running tally of major tech layoffs this year where companies explicitly pointed to AI as a reason — and the list keeps getting longer, including Microsoft's cut of roughly 3,200 jobs in its Xbox division. Whether AI is truly replacing the work or serving as convenient cover for cost-cutting is hotly debated. Either way, "because of AI" has become one of the defining phrases of this year's job market.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

7. Zuckerberg Tells Staff AI Agents Are Moving Slower Than He Hoped

In an internal address, Mark Zuckerberg admitted that AI agents — programs meant to complete multi-step tasks on their own — haven't advanced as quickly as he expected. It's a notable dose of candor from a CEO who has spent billions hiring top AI researchers and reorganizing Meta around superintelligence. The comment echoes a broader industry reality check: today's agents are useful, but still far from the autonomous digital workers the hype promised.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

item.title: Edition #20: Google to Pay SpaceX $920M a Month for AI Compute; Microsoft Builds Its Own AI Models; White House Signs AI Executive Order
item.description: Google agrees to pay SpaceX roughly $920 million a month to rent AI computing power. Microsoft unveils seven of its own AI models to lean less on OpenAI. The White House signs an executive order to speed up AI while guarding against its risks. Cognition, the maker of AI "software engineer" Devin, raises $1 billion at a $26 billion valuation. Nvidia releases its most powerful free, open AI model yet. China's DeepSeek makes a 75% price cut permanent, escalating the AI price war. And a new AI tool helps eye doctors catch disease hidden in hundreds of retinal scans.
item.content:encoded:
Today's Blast — 7 Stories

1. Google Will Pay SpaceX $920 Million a Month to Rent AI Computing Power

Google has agreed to pay SpaceX roughly $920 million every month — about $30 billion over the life of the deal — to rent access to around 110,000 high-end AI chips housed in data centers tied to Elon Musk's companies. Google says it needs the extra "bridge" capacity because demand for its Gemini AI tools has outstripped what its own data centers can supply. The unusual arrangement, struck just before SpaceX's stock-market debut, shows how desperate even the biggest tech firms have become for the raw computing muscle that modern AI requires.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

2. Microsoft Builds Its Own AI Models to Depend Less on OpenAI

At its annual developer conference, Microsoft unveiled seven AI models it built entirely in-house — including its first home-grown "reasoning" model — signaling a push to rely less on its partner OpenAI. The company says its own models are cheaper to run, an appealing pitch as businesses look to cut the cost of using AI. Microsoft stressed it isn't cutting ties with OpenAI, whose technology still powers many of its products, but it clearly wants more options of its own.

Source: CNBC · Read more →

3. White House Signs Executive Order to Speed Up AI While Guarding Its Risks

The White House signed an executive order aimed at accelerating American AI development while shoring up defenses against the security risks that powerful AI can create. The order sets up a government "clearinghouse" to help find and fix software vulnerabilities, and asks leading AI companies to voluntarily give the government an early look at their most advanced models before public release. Notably, it explicitly stops short of creating any mandatory license or permit to build or release AI systems.

Source: The White House · Read more →

4. The Startup Behind AI 'Software Engineer' Devin Raises $1 Billion

Cognition, the maker of an AI "software engineer" called Devin that can write and fix code largely on its own, raised more than $1 billion at a $26 billion valuation — more than double its worth just eight months ago. The company says corporate use of Devin has grown 50% month over month, with customers including Goldman Sachs, Mercedes-Benz, and NASA. The eye-popping round captures both investor excitement and growing anxiety about what increasingly capable coding tools mean for software jobs.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

5. Nvidia Releases Its Most Powerful 'Open' AI Model Yet — Free for Anyone to Use

Nvidia released Nemotron 3 Ultra, a powerful new AI model that the company is giving away for free — publishing not just the model but the data and recipes used to build it. It is now the most capable "open" AI model made in the United States, though it still trails the strongest open model from China. Freely available models like this let smaller companies and researchers build advanced AI tools without paying to use the big commercial systems.

Source: Artificial Analysis · Read more →

6. China's DeepSeek Makes a 75% Price Cut Permanent, Escalating the AI Price War

China's DeepSeek announced that a temporary 75% discount on its flagship V4-Pro model is now permanent, making it dramatically cheaper than comparable models from OpenAI and Anthropic. The company can afford the low prices partly because its models are tuned to run on Chinese-made Huawei chips rather than scarce, pricey Nvidia hardware. The move intensifies a global price war that keeps driving down the cost of using AI — welcome news for businesses and developers, painful for competitors.

Source: Engadget · Read more →

7. New AI Tool Helps Eye Doctors Catch Disease Hidden in Hundreds of Scans

Researchers at Washington University in St. Louis built an experimental AI system that helps eye doctors sift through the hundreds of images produced in a single retinal scan, flagging subtle signs of disease faster and more reliably than a manual review. Because catching these clues early can prevent vision loss, tools like this could make screening quicker and surface problems doctors might otherwise miss. It's a concrete example of AI quietly improving routine medical care.

Source: Newswise · Read more →

item.title: Edition #19: Apple Unveils a Gemini-Powered Siri; Nvidia & SK Hynix Team Up on AI Memory; Anthropic Files to Go Public
item.description: Apple unveils a rebuilt, Gemini-powered Siri at WWDC and lets users choose their AI assistant. Nvidia and SK Hynix team up to build the memory behind AI "factories." Anthropic raises $65 billion and files to go public ahead of OpenAI. Europe moves to simplify its AI rules as US states press ahead with their own. SpaceX heads toward the largest IPO in history, now with xAI on board. Memory chipmakers hit $1 trillion as AI reshapes the hardware race. And Big Tech is on track to spend over $700 billion building AI this year.
item.content:encoded:
Today's Blast — 7 Stories

1. Apple Unveils a Gemini-Powered Siri at WWDC — and Lets You Choose Your AI

Apple used its WWDC keynote on Monday to reveal the long-awaited rebuild of Siri, now running on a custom version of Google's Gemini that Apple is reportedly paying about $1 billion a year to license. The new assistant can hold a conversation, act on what's on your screen, and carry out multi-step tasks across apps — and a new Extensions system lets users pick ChatGPT, Gemini, or Anthropic's Claude as the brain behind it. The event also marked a milestone for the company, widely reported as CEO Tim Cook's final keynote before a planned leadership handoff.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

2. Nvidia and SK Hynix Team Up to Build the Memory Behind AI 'Factories'

Chip giant Nvidia and South Korea's SK Hynix announced a multi-year partnership to develop next-generation memory for the massive data centers — now often called "AI factories" — that power tools like ChatGPT. The two will co-design memory for Nvidia's upcoming systems and even use AI to speed up the design and manufacturing of the chips themselves. The deal deepens a relationship that has helped make SK Hynix one of the most important suppliers in the global AI supply chain.

Source: Nvidia · Read more →

3. Anthropic Raises $65 Billion and Files to Go Public Ahead of OpenAI

Claude maker Anthropic closed a $65 billion funding round that values the company at roughly $965 billion, then quietly filed paperwork to go public — putting it on track to beat rival OpenAI to the stock market. The company says its annual revenue run-rate has crossed $47 billion and expects its first-ever operating profit this quarter. It's a striking sign of how quickly money is pouring into the handful of firms building the most advanced AI.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

4. Europe Moves to Simplify Its AI Rules as US States Press Ahead

European lawmakers agreed to streamline parts of the EU's landmark AI Act, easing some deadlines and paperwork for businesses while keeping its core safeguards — including new bans on tools that create non-consensual explicit images. In the United States, the picture is messier: a federal push to override state AI laws hasn't passed, leaving states like Colorado moving ahead with their own rules and companies unsure which requirements will ultimately stick. Together the moves show governments still scrambling to set the ground rules for AI.

Source: Council of the EU · Read more →

5. SpaceX Heads Toward the Largest IPO in History — With xAI on Board

SpaceX is racing toward what would be the biggest stock-market debut ever, with pricing expected this week and trading set to begin under the ticker "SPCX." Following its merger with Elon Musk's AI startup xAI, the company now combines rockets and frontier AI under one roof, and is reportedly targeting a valuation of more than $1.7 trillion. Investors are watching closely: SpaceX's debut is expected to set the tone for a wave of giant AI listings, including OpenAI and Anthropic, later this year.

Source: Yahoo Finance · Read more →

6. Memory Chipmakers Hit $1 Trillion as AI Reshapes the Hardware Race

The companies that make the memory chips inside AI servers are suddenly Wall Street darlings, with SK Hynix and Micron each crossing $1 trillion in market value as demand outstrips supply. For years the spotlight was on Nvidia's graphics chips, but the AI boom has revealed that fast, abundant memory is just as essential — and far harder to produce quickly. The surge underscores how the scramble to build AI is rippling far beyond the best-known names.

Source: CNBC · Read more →

7. Big Tech Is on Track to Spend Over $700 Billion Building AI This Year

Microsoft, Google, Amazon, and Meta are collectively expected to pour at least $700 billion into AI data centers and infrastructure in 2026, and when private firms like OpenAI and Anthropic are added in, total industry spending could top $1 trillion. New figures show venture funding for foundational AI startups in early 2026 was already double the entire prior year. The numbers capture the sheer scale of the buildout — and the bet that demand for AI will keep climbing.

Source: Crunchbase News · Read more →

item.title: Edition #18: Apple's WWDC Brings Gemini-Powered Siri; ChatGPT Hits 1 Billion Users; Sanders Targets AI Ownership
item.description: Apple's WWDC opens Monday with a rebuilt, Gemini-powered Siri at its center. ChatGPT becomes the fastest app ever to reach one billion monthly users. Bernie Sanders proposes giving the public a 50% stake in big AI companies. OpenAI expands its Codex assistant beyond coders to sales, finance, and design teams. Uber and WeRide launch Spain's first commercial robotaxi pilot in Madrid. And a new report catalogs 37 manipulative "dark patterns" in major AI chatbots.
item.content:encoded:
Today's Blast — 6 Stories

1. Apple's WWDC Opens Monday With a Long-Awaited, Gemini-Powered Siri

Apple takes the stage Monday for what may be the most consequential keynote in its AI history, with the centerpiece a complete rebuild of Siri. Reports say the new assistant will run on a custom 1.2-trillion-parameter version of Google's Gemini — roughly eight times larger than anything Apple built in-house — which Apple is paying about $1 billion a year to license. The revamped Siri is expected to handle multi-step tasks, understand on-screen context, and even hand questions off to chatbots like Claude.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

2. ChatGPT Becomes the Fastest App Ever to Reach 1 Billion Monthly Users

ChatGPT has crossed one billion monthly active users on its app, hitting the milestone faster than any product before it — outpacing the early growth of TikTok, Instagram, and YouTube, according to Sensor Tower data reported by Reuters. It reached the mark roughly three years after launch, a sign that consumer AI has moved from novelty to everyday software. Rivals remain far smaller: Claude sits around 56 million monthly users, though it is growing several times faster year over year.

Source: Reuters · Read more →

3. Bernie Sanders Proposes Giving the Public a 50% Stake in Big AI Companies

Senator Bernie Sanders unveiled plans for an "American AI Sovereign Wealth Fund," a bill that would require the largest AI firms — including OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI — to transfer half their stock to a public fund. The proceeds would be paid out to Americans as direct cash payments, with later revenue funding programs like health care and housing. The idea is a long shot legislatively, but it lands as figures across the political spectrum begin debating public ownership of AI's enormous gains.

Source: Fortune · Read more →

4. OpenAI Expands Codex Beyond Coders to Sales, Finance, and Design Teams

OpenAI is pushing its Codex AI assistant well past its programming roots, releasing six role-specific versions aimed at non-developers in sales, data analytics, product design, creative work, and finance. The company also introduced "Codex Sites," which can turn a written prompt into a working dashboard or web app. OpenAI says more than five million people now use Codex weekly, and non-coders are its fastest-growing group.

Source: OpenAI · Read more →

5. Uber and WeRide Launch Spain's First Commercial Robotaxi Pilot in Madrid

Uber and Chinese self-driving firm WeRide announced Spain's first commercial robotaxi service, bringing autonomous rides to Madrid through the regular Uber app later this year. The fleet will start with trained safety operators on board before scaling toward fully driverless service, in partnership with the regional government. It marks the duo's first move into Europe and the fourth of fifteen cities they have pledged to reach by 2030.

Source: The Next Web · Read more →

6. New Report Finds 37 Manipulative 'Dark Patterns' in Major AI Chatbots

A new study from the Center for Democracy & Technology catalogs 37 deceptive design tricks baked into popular AI chatbots, including ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and companion apps like Replika and Character.AI. The researchers warn these "dark patterns" can quietly maximize data collection, foster emotional dependence, and make it hard to delete an account. The report offers a taxonomy meant to push designers and regulators toward healthier defaults.

Source: 404 Media · Read more →

item.title: Edition #17: Anthropic Nears $900B Valuation; Google I/O Today; Musk Loses OpenAI Lawsuit
item.description: Anthropic is in talks to raise $30 billion at a $900 billion valuation. Google I/O opens today with Gemini 4.0 and persistent AI agents expected. A jury throws out Elon Musk's lawsuit against Sam Altman and OpenAI. Anthropic's Q1 revenue grew 80x year-over-year, putting its ARR above $44 billion. A Harvard study finds OpenAI's o1 model outperforms emergency-room doctors on diagnoses. And Fortune warns the AI shock is coming for white-collar workers, much like the China shock came for factories.
item.content:encoded:
Today's Blast — 6 Stories

1. Anthropic in Talks to Raise $30 Billion at a $900 Billion Valuation

Claude maker Anthropic is closing in on a roughly $30 billion fundraising round at a pre-money valuation north of $900 billion, co-led by Sequoia, Dragoneer, Greenoaks, and Altimeter. The deal — expected to wrap by the end of this month — would nearly triple Anthropic's $380 billion valuation from February and could vault it past OpenAI as the most valuable private AI company in the world.

Source: Bloomberg · Read more →

2. Google I/O Kicks Off Today With Gemini 4.0 and Persistent AI Agents Expected

Google's annual I/O developer conference opens this morning at Shoreline Amphitheatre. Expected announcements include a next-generation Gemini model (rumored as Gemini 4.0), a unified "Omni" system that generates text, images and video, persistent AI agents that can complete tasks across apps, and a preview of Android XR smart glasses.

Source: Google I/O 2026 · Read more →

3. Jury Throws Out Elon Musk's Lawsuit Against Sam Altman and OpenAI

A federal jury in Oakland took less than two hours to reject Elon Musk's lawsuit accusing Sam Altman, Greg Brockman, OpenAI and Microsoft of "stealing a charity" by converting the lab into a for-profit. The nine-member panel ruled unanimously that Musk waited too long to sue. Musk called the verdict a "calendar technicality" and vowed to appeal.

Source: NPR · Read more →

4. Anthropic Q1 Revenue Grew 80x Year-Over-Year, ARR Now Above $44 Billion

Anthropic disclosed that its first-quarter revenue was 80 times higher than the same period a year ago, pushing annualized revenue above $44 billion and narrowing the gap with OpenAI's $25 billion run rate. The number of customers spending at least $1 million a year doubled to more than 1,000 in just two months.

Source: The Information · Read more →

5. Harvard Study: OpenAI's o1 Model Outperforms ER Doctors on Diagnoses

A new Science paper from Harvard Medical School and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center found that OpenAI's o1 reasoning model matched or exceeded experienced physicians on 76 real emergency-room cases in Boston. The AI did especially well on rare diseases and complex case management — using only the same electronic health records the doctors saw.

Source: Fortune · Read more →

6. Fortune: The AI Shock Is Coming for White-Collar Workers, Much Like the China Shock

A new Fortune analysis warns that AI is poised to do to coastal knowledge work what the China shock did to Midwestern factories — except the pain will be concentrated in urban centers full of well-paid analysts, marketers and coders. Outplacement firm Challenger has already tied 49,000 layoffs to AI automation in 2026 alone, nearly matching all of 2025.

Source: Fortune · Read more →

item.title: Edition #16: Jane Street Commits $7B to CoreWeave; PwC Finds AI Gains Go to Top 20%; EU Frozen Out of Mythos
item.description: Jane Street commits $7 billion to CoreWeave in an AI cloud and equity deal. PwC finds 74% of AI's economic gains go to just 20% of companies. EU regulators are frozen out of Anthropic's Mythos cybersecurity model. Human scientists still outperform AI agents on complex tasks. The DOE's AI push squeezes traditional research funding. UChicago partners with Microsoft and NVIDIA to accelerate Midwest AI startups.
item.content:encoded:
Today's Blast — 6 Stories

1. Jane Street Commits $7 Billion to CoreWeave in Massive AI Cloud and Equity Deal

Wall Street trading giant Jane Street is going all-in on AI infrastructure, committing roughly $6 billion to use CoreWeave's AI cloud platform plus a separate $1 billion equity stake at $109 per share. The deal gives Jane Street access to NVIDIA's next-gen Vera Rubin chips across multiple data centers. It's CoreWeave's third mega-deal in April alone, following $21 billion from Meta and a multibillion-dollar agreement with Anthropic.

Source: Quartz · Read more →

2. PwC Study: 74% of AI's Economic Gains Are Being Captured by Just 20% of Companies

A sweeping new PwC study of 1,217 senior executives finds that a small elite of companies is pulling dramatically ahead in the AI race. The top 20% are generating 7.2 times more AI-driven revenue and efficiency gains than the average competitor — and they're doing it by using AI to reinvent their business models, not just cut costs.

Source: PwC · Read more →

3. EU Regulators Frozen Out of Anthropic's Mythos Cybersecurity Model

European cyber agencies are largely being shut out of Anthropic's powerful Mythos model, which can find and exploit software vulnerabilities faster than most human hackers. Access has been limited to U.S. tech giants under a program called Project Glasswing. Only Germany has started talks so far, while the UK's AI Safety Institute has already been allowed to test it.

Source: CSO Online · Read more →

4. Human Scientists Still Outperform AI Agents on Complex Tasks, Nature Reports

Despite the hype around autonomous AI agents, a major new analysis in Nature finds that human researchers still significantly outperform them on complex scientific workflows. Many labs have started deploying AI agents to run experiments and analyze data autonomously, but the report is skeptical about real-world performance.

Source: Nature · Read more →

5. DOE's $293 Million AI Push Is Squeezing Funding for Traditional Science

The Department of Energy's new Genesis Mission — a $320 million initiative to apply AI across scientific disciplines — is coming at a steep cost to traditional research. Nuclear physics grants have already fallen 18%, and redirecting another 10% to Genesis means roughly one-third of expiring grants won't be renewed this year.

Source: Science · Read more →

6. UChicago Partners with Microsoft and NVIDIA to Accelerate Midwest AI Startups

The University of Chicago announced a new partnership with Microsoft and NVIDIA aimed at boosting AI startups in the Midwest. Participating companies will get up to $350,000 in startup credits, access to AI models, connections to Bay Area investors, and support from both NVIDIA's Inception and Microsoft for Startups programs.

Source: UChicago Polsky Center · Read more →

item.title: Edition #15: Stanford AI Index Shows China Closing Gap; Anthropic Mythos Alarms Cybersecurity World; OpenAI Shuts Down Sora
item.description: Stanford's 2026 AI Index reveals China has nearly erased the U.S. lead in AI while generative AI adoption outpaces the internet. Anthropic's Mythos model finds thousands of unpatched vulnerabilities, prompting a restricted release to just 40 organizations. OpenAI is shutting down Sora amid $15M/day costs. Google releases Gemma 4 under Apache 2.0. U.S. utilities plan $1.4 trillion in spending driven by AI data centers. The GSA turns to AI after losing 40% of its workforce. NVIDIA unveils quantum AI models.
item.content:encoded:
Today's Blast — 7 Stories

1. Stanford's 2026 AI Index: China Nearly Erases U.S. Lead, AI Adoption Outpaces the Internet

Stanford's annual AI Index dropped today and the numbers are staggering. Generative AI hit 53% population adoption in just three years — faster than the personal computer or the internet. AI agents now handle real-world tasks with a 77% success rate, up from 20% last year. But the geopolitical headline is bigger: China has nearly erased the U.S. lead in AI model performance, driven by its open-source community. Meanwhile, the number of AI researchers moving to the U.S. has dropped 89% since 2017.

Source: Stanford HAI · Read more →

2. Anthropic's Mythos Model Finds Thousands of Unpatched Vulnerabilities, Alarming Cybersecurity World

Anthropic's new Mythos model is so good at hacking that the company is only sharing it with 40 handpicked organizations, including Microsoft, Google, and JPMorgan Chase. In testing, Mythos autonomously found and chained together flaws in the Linux kernel that would give a hacker full control of a machine. Over 99% of the vulnerabilities it found haven't been patched yet.

Source: Fortune · Read more →

3. OpenAI Shutting Down Sora as the AI Video App Burns $15 Million a Day

OpenAI is pulling the plug on Sora, its AI video generator, with the app closing April 26 and the API following in September. Despite over a million downloads in its first week, active users cratered to under 500,000 while compute costs ballooned to an estimated $15 million per day. Disney also walked away from a planned $1 billion investment tied to the project.

Source: TechCrunch · Read more →

4. Google Releases Gemma 4 — Its Most Capable Open Models Yet, Now Under Apache 2.0

Google just dropped Gemma 4, a family of four open models purpose-built for reasoning and agentic workflows. The headline: a 31-billion-parameter model that outperforms rivals 20 times its size, with 256K context windows and support for over 140 languages. Gemma 4 ships under the Apache 2.0 license — a big shift from Google's previous restrictive licensing.

Source: Google Blog · Read more →

5. U.S. Utilities Plan $1.4 Trillion Spending Surge as AI Data Centers Strain the Grid

America's biggest utilities are gearing up for a historic investment cycle. Investor-owned utilities have increased their five-year capital plans by 27% to $1.4 trillion, driven largely by AI data center construction. Nearly half of that spending could get passed on to residential customers.

Source: Fortune · Read more →

6. GSA Turns to AI to Automate One Million Work Hours After Losing 40% of Its Workforce

The General Services Administration has lost nearly 40% of its workforce and is now turning to AI to fill the gap, with plans to automate roughly one million work hours. It's one of the most concrete examples yet of the federal government replacing human workers with AI systems.

Source: Federal News Network · Read more →

7. NVIDIA Unveils Ising — Open-Source Quantum AI Models for Building Quantum Processors

NVIDIA announced Ising, a new family of open-source AI models designed to accelerate the development of quantum processors. The models serve as an AI control plane for quantum hardware, helping engineers design and optimize quantum chips using machine learning.

Source: CIO · Read more →
